title: The Bound You Picked: Tolerances for a Test With Noise in It, and How Many Samples It Takes to See a Bug

questions.question: A test averages 100 noisy readings of spread 1 and uses a bound of 0.1, picked because the first run's error was 0.013. How often does it fail?
options: About a third of the time: the average itself varies by about 0.1, so a bound of one spread is exceeded 31.8 percent of the time

questions.question: What is the spread of the average of n readings, each with noise of spread 1?
options: About 1 divided by the square root of n: 0.1 for 100 readings

questions.question: How often did a bound of three spreads and of six spreads fail over 10000 seeds?
questions.explanation: Three spreads is about one in 400; six is about one in five hundred million.

questions.question: Why is one in 400 not good enough for a test in a large suite?
options: A suite of three thousand such tests fails nearly every run, each on a different test
questions.explanation: Each test on its own passes a thousand times in a row.

questions.question: With 100 readings and a bound of 0.6, how often is a bias of 0.3 seen, and a bias of 1.0?
options: 0.1 percent and 100 percent: the bound is too wide for that bug at that length
questions.explanation: A bias of 0.5 was seen 15.1 percent of the time.

questions.question: How many readings does a bias of 0.3 need, at noise 1 and six spreads, and what did the suite see?
options: 1600, seen in 2000 of 2000 runs with 0 false alarms in 10000
questions.explanation: Twice the noise needs four times the readings.
